# Convert Video to Animated GIF

- Route: `/tools/convert-video-to-animated-gif`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `video`
- Slug: `convert-video-to-animated-gif`

## Summary

Turn short MP4, WebM, MOV, or MKV clips into shareable animated GIFs in seconds. (Video tools)

## Details

An animated GIF is a stack of indexed-colour frames, 256 colours at most per palette, with no inter-frame compression beyond simple run-length coding. That is why a GIF of a few seconds can outweigh an MP4 of a minute, and why making a good one is mostly about choosing width, frame rate and palette size. This page runs a two-stage pipeline: FFmpeg scales the video to the width you set and samples it at your frame rate, writing a raw GIF, then gifsicle re-quantises the palette to your colour count, sets the frame delay and optimises the frames so only changed pixels are stored. The defaults are tuned for screen recordings: 900 pixels wide, 12 frames per second, 128 colours.
### What it does
- Scales the clip to a chosen width (16 to 2000 px) with the height computed from the aspect ratio and rounded to a multiple of 4.
- Samples the source at a chosen frame rate (1 to 50 fps; 12 by default) with FFmpeg.
- Quantises each frame to a palette of 2 to 256 colours (128 by default) and optimises inter-frame storage with gifsicle at level 1 to 3.
- Sets the frame delay in hundredths of a second, which decides playback speed independently of the sampling rate.
- Honours a trim range from the converter form so only the selected seconds become frames.
### How to use it
1. Upload a video and pick GIF: GIF is already selected as the output on this page; the Quality control is disabled because it does not apply.
2. Trim to a few seconds: Use the trim control to keep the moment you want; every extra second is 12 more frames at the default rate.
3. Set width, frame rate, colours and delay: The Animated GIF Settings panel starts at 900 px, 12 fps, 128 colours, delay 3, optimise 3.
4. FFmpeg samples, gifsicle optimises: ffmpeg scale=W:-4 -pix_fmt rgb8 -r FPS, then gifsicle --optimize --delay --colors --interlace.
5. Download the GIF: A standard looping GIF that chat apps and browsers play inline.
### Technical details
- Stage one is ffmpeg -i input [-ss START -t DURATION] -vf scale=W:-4 -pix_fmt rgb8 -r FPS -f gif raw.gif (convertVideoToGIF in converter.go). The -4 asks for a height that keeps the aspect ratio and is divisible by 4; rgb8 is an 8-bit indexed intermediate that stage two re-quantises.
- Stage two is gifsicle --optimize=L --delay=D --colors C --interlace raw.gif -o output.gif. Optimise level 3 is the slowest and smallest: it stores only the rectangle of pixels that changed between frames, which is why a screencast with a static toolbar compresses far better than a panning camera shot.
- The delay is applied to every frame after sampling and is independent of the sampling rate. At the default 12 fps and delay 3 (30 ms per frame) a clip plays about 2.8 times faster than real time; set the delay to 8 (80 ms, 12.5 fps) for roughly real-time playback at 12 fps, or 10 at 10 fps.
- A width typed into the main Width field of the converter overrides the GIF panel width, so power users can keep one knob. Colours are clamped to 2 to 256 by the form; a GIF palette can never exceed 256.
- There is no palettegen pass in FFmpeg here; palette quality comes from gifsicle --colors, which builds one optimised palette for the whole animation. Photographic clips with smooth gradients benefit from 256 colours; flat UI footage looks identical at 64.
- The gifsicle stage runs under a 6 hour timeout, and the upload also receives the automated content analysis that standard conversions get, since GIF is a format of the regular video converter.
### When not to use it
Do not make a GIF of anything longer than about 10 seconds or with photographic motion across the whole frame; the format has no real inter-frame compression, so such clips become tens of megabytes while an MP4 or WebM of the same thing is a tenth of the size. Do not use GIF when colour fidelity matters, since every frame is limited to a 256-colour palette and gradients band. If the destination plays video inline, a compressed MP4 is better in every way. And if you need audio, a GIF cannot carry it at all.
### Use cases
- Bug reproductions: Record the screen, trim to the failure, and drop the GIF in the ticket.
- README and documentation demos: Show a feature in motion where a video embed is not allowed.
- Reaction clips: Cut 3 seconds from a video and share it anywhere that accepts images.
- Email previews: A small looping GIF linking to the full video, where video itself will not play.
### FAQ
Q: Why does my GIF play faster than the original video?
A: The frame delay is set after sampling and defaults to 3 hundredths of a second, which is about 33 frames per second of playback for frames sampled at 12 per second. Set the delay to 8 at 12 fps, or 10 at 10 fps, for real-time playback.
Q: How do I make the GIF smaller?
A: In order of effect: trim to fewer seconds, lower the width (480 is plenty for chat), lower the frame rate to 8 or 10, and reduce colours to 64 on flat UI footage. Keep optimise at 3; levels 1 and 2 only trade size for speed.
Q: How many colours should I use?
A: 128, the default, suits most screen recordings. Flat interfaces look identical at 64 and save bytes. Photographic footage with gradients wants 256, which is the GIF maximum.
Q: Can I pick which part of the video becomes the GIF?
A: Yes. Use the trim control in the converter to set a start and end; only that range is sampled. Shorter is better, since every second adds frames at the chosen rate.
Q: Will the GIF loop, and does it keep the sound?
A: It loops, as GIFs do by default in every player. It cannot carry audio; the format has no sound track. Extract the audio separately if you need it.
Q: What is the largest GIF I can make?
A: The form allows up to 2000 px wide, 50 fps and 256 colours, but a GIF at those settings grows enormous fast. Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.

## Routing

When to send a visitor here: Send visitors here when they want to turn a short MP4, WebM, MOV or MKV clip into an animated GIF for chat, docs or a reaction image, with control over width, frame rate and palette size. Phrasings like "make a GIF from this video" or "clip to GIF" fit.
When to send them elsewhere: For long clips, full-colour footage, or anything that needs sound, a compressed video is better: use Compress Video (compress-video). To shorten the clip first, use Video Trimmer (video-trimmer). To animate vector artwork rather than footage, use Motion (motion).
Related tools: video-trimmer (cut the clip down before making the GIF); compress-video (smaller, better-looking video alternative); crop-video (frame only the part you want); content-studio (edit a longer piece with titles)
